site.look: 1. Review the daily inspection log for the audit period and count entries per day; if practical, observe or shadow one inspection round in progress. Pass = ≥3 logged inspections every day with no unexplained gaps; fail = days with fewer than 3 inspections and no documented reason or catch-up inspection. 2. Request the weekly inspection record and, during the walkabout, check the named high-load areas (departure taxiways, stands, take-off taxiways, intersections, touchdown zones) for evidence of recent detailed inspection (e.g. chalk marks, freshly noted findings). Pass = weekly record demonstrably covers and emphasises the named high-load areas; fail = weekly record generic, with no clear focus on those areas. 3. Check whether the current annual inspection report's scope still covers all pavements presently in use, with no new/expanded areas omitted. 4. During the walkabout, check for any recently cut grass areas and confirm clippings have been fully removed (a specific §8.8.3 trigger); request the most recent special inspection records tied to any recent complaint, construction activity or unusual event and check team composition. Pass = special inspections documented for all applicable trigger events with qualified personnel; fail = a trigger event (e.g. recent grass cutting) with no corresponding special inspection record, or no evidence of qualified personnel on the team.
site.pass: Three logged manoeuvring-area inspections every day with no unexplained gap, the apron audit twice a month, the bay inspection daily during turnaround, and the most recent annual inspection signed by a qualified civil engineer.

demo.proves: Not whether a log exists but whether the rounds actually happen at the stated frequency — which is why the walkabout says shadow one.

site.pass: An incident register with near-misses in it, notification inside ACSA's clock (12 hours for a fatality, 24 hours for a Section 24 injury or LTI, 36 hours for Section 24(c) equipment failure, 72 hours for a near miss), Annexure 1 submitted to the DoL, investigations closed with their corrective actions, and a trend review. The real test is asking maintenance staff how they report a near-miss and finding the examples they describe in the register.

demo.ask: 3. What is ACSA's target timeframe (days/weeks) for closing out corrective actions, and how many open items currently exceed it? 4. How often is incident/near-miss data formally reviewed for trends, and who is accountable for that review?
demo.proves: Ask maintenance staff how they report a near-miss and check those examples are in the register. A mismatch is the finding, and no document shows it.
